chapter_title: Identification and Classification of Soil and Rock

sections.title: Soil Index Properties
sections.summary: Key soil index properties: grain-size distribution (Cu = D60/D10, Cc = D30²/(D10×D60); percent fines = % passing #200 sieve); water content (wn 0–20% for sands, 10–40%+ for clays/silts); unit weight (γt, γd, γsat); Atterberg limits (LL, PL, PI = LL-PL, LI = (wn-PL)/PI, Activity = PI/CF). Organic content: high water retention, high compressibility, possible high corrosion. Carbonate: may act as cementing agent. Clay mineralogy influences: SSA, surface charge, and cation exchange capacity; Activity 0.4 (kaolinite) to 8+ (montmorillonite).
sections.body:
Grain-size distribution: Measured by sieve analysis (coarse-grained) and hydrometer (fine-grained per ASTM D7928/formerly D422). Coefficient of uniformity Cu = D60/D10; coefficient of curvature Cc = D30²/(D10 × D60). Well-graded soils have Cu ≥ 4 (gravels) or ≥ 6 (sands) and 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3. Percent fines = % passing #200 sieve.

Water content: wn = mw/ms. Sands: 0–20%; silts and inorganic clays: 10–40%; soft and sensitive clays, organic soils: wn can exceed 100%.

Unit weight: γt = Wt/V; γd = Ws/V; γt = γd(1+wn). Specific gravity Gs for most soils is 2.6–2.8 (AASHTO T100, ASTM D854).

Atterberg limits: LL per AASHTO T89/ASTM D4318 (Casagrande cup: water content at 25 blows) or fall cone (British standard; 20 mm penetration at LL). PL per AASHTO T90/ASTM D4318 (thread method: crumbles at 3.2 mm diameter). PI = LL - PL (Eq 4.12). LI = (wn - PL)/PI (Eq 4.13).

Activity (Eq 4.16): A = PI/CF where CF = clay-size fraction (% < 0.002 mm). Activity ranges: 0.4 (kaolinite), 0.9 (illite), 7–8+ (montmorillonite). High activity = high swelling potential.

Clay mineralogy characterization: X-ray diffraction (XRD) identifies minerals from interatomic plane spacing. Specific surface area (SSA) distinguishes clay mineral types; SSA ranges: kaolinite 5–50 m²/g; illite 50–200 m²/g; montmorillonite 200–800 m²/g.

Carbonate content: Calcium and calcium-magnesium carbonates can act as cementing agents. High carbonate soils or rocks may dissolve and create voids (karst hazard). Organic content: Organic soils have high water content, primary and secondary compressibility, and corrosion potential.
key_points: Cu = D60/D10; Cc = D30²/(D10×D60); well-graded: Cu ≥ 4 (gravel) or ≥ 6 (sand), 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3
PI = LL - PL; LI = (wn - PL)/PI; Activity = PI/CF (clay fraction < 0.002 mm)
Activity: 0.4 kaolinite → 0.9 illite → 7-8+ montmorillonite — indicator of swelling potential
SSA for clay mineral identification: kaolinite 5–50 m²/g; illite 50–200; montmorillonite 200–800
Organic soils: high wn (>100% possible), high compressibility, potential corrosion risk

sections.title: Soil Classification Systems and In Situ Identification
sections.summary: USCS (ASTM D2487): primary designation G/S/M/C/O/Pt; based on >50% #200 (fine-grained) or <50% (coarse); secondary from Cu, Cc (coarse) or Casagrande plasticity chart (fine). AASHTO (ASTM D3282): A-1 to A-8; Group Index from gradation and Atterberg limits. CPT soil behavior type (SBT): original Robertson et al. (1986) chart uses qc and friction ratio Rf = fs/qc × 100%; normalized SBTn uses Q and F. Ic-RW = √[(3.47-logQ)² + (logF+1.22)²] (Eq 4.28); Ic > 2.6 indicates fine-grained. DMT material index ID = (p1-p0)/(p0-u0) distinguishes soft cohesive to dense sand.
sections.body:
USCS classification: Based on grain-size analysis and Atterberg limits. Primary symbol based on >50% passing #200 (fine-grained) or <50% (coarse). For coarse-grained soils, secondary designation from Cu and Cc (W = well-graded, P = poorly graded). For fine-grained soils, secondary designation from Casagrande Plasticity Chart: L or H plasticity, C (clay) or M (silt) based on position relative to A-line.

AASHTO classification (ASTM D3282): Groups A-1 through A-8. Group Index (Eq 4.22): GI = (F-35)[0.2+0.005(LL-40)] + 0.01(F-15)(PI-10), where F = percent passing #200. GI ranges from 0 (good subgrade) to 20+ (very poor).

Table 4-14: Approximate comparison between USCS and AASHTO systems.

CPT soil behavior type (SBT): Robertson et al. (1986) chart uses qc (tip resistance) and Rf = fs/qc × 100% (friction ratio) — Eq 4.24. Updated Robertson (2010) uses normalized qt and F. Soil behavior type index (Robertson and Wride 1998, Eq 4.28): Ic-RW = √[(3.47-logQ)² + (logF+1.22)²] where Q = (qt-σvo)/σ'vo and F = fs/(qt-σvo)×100%. Ic > 2.6 generally indicates fine-grained behavior; Ic < 2.6 indicates coarse-grained. Extended per Robertson (2010) as Ic-JB for normalized CPTU.

CPT corrected cone resistance: qt = qc + u2(1-a) (Eq 4.23) where a = net area ratio from calibration.

DMT material index: ID = (p1-p0)/(p0-u0). ID < 0.1 = soft clay; 0.1–0.35 = clay; 0.35–0.9 = silty clay/clayey silt; 0.9–1.8 = silt; 1.8–3.3 = sandy silt/silty sand; >3.3 = sand.
key_points: USCS (ASTM D2487): G/S (coarse, >50% retained #200); M/C (fine, >50% passing #200); W/P from Cu/Cc
AASHTO Group Index: GI from F (% passing #200), LL, PI; higher GI = worse subgrade material
CPT friction ratio: Rf = fs/qc × 100%; lower Rf = granular; higher Rf = cohesive
DMT material index ID: < 0.35 = clay; 0.35–1.8 = silt/mixed; > 1.8 = sand

sections.title: Rock Identification and Classification
sections.summary: RQD (ASTM D6032) = sum of pieces >100 mm / total core length × 100%; RQD 0–25 = very poor, 25–50 = poor, 50–75 = fair, 75–90 = good, 90–100 = excellent. Intact rock classified by type (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic), mineralogy, texture (grain size), and relative strength (R0 extremely weak ~35–150 psi to R6 extremely strong >30,000 psi). Rock mass classification via RMR and GSI systems (Chapter 9). Automated drilling parameters (feed rate, penetration rate, thrust, torque, rotation speed) provide supplemental characterization but are not yet standard practice.
sections.body:
Rock quality designation (RQD): Developed by Deere and Deere (1988). RQD = (Σ lengths of intact core pieces >100 mm) / total core length × 100% (ASTM D6032). RQD ratings: 0–25 Very Poor; 25–50 Poor; 50–75 Fair; 75–90 Good; 90–100 Excellent. RQD reflects degree of natural fracturing in rock mass.

Rock type classification: Three main types: (1) igneous — formed by solidification of molten material; classified by mineral composition and texture (intrusive vs. extrusive). Examples: granite/rhyolite; gabbro/basalt. (2) Sedimentary — deposited and lithified sediments; examples: sandstone, shale, limestone. (3) Metamorphic — formed by transformation under heat and pressure; examples: schist, gneiss, marble. Rock type tables: Table 4-19 (NRCS classification), Table 4-20 (igneous), Tables for sedimentary and metamorphic.

Grain size descriptions: Very fine-grained (<0.075 mm), fine-grained (0.075–0.425 mm), medium-grained (0.425–2 mm), coarse-grained (2–10 mm), very coarse-grained (>10 mm) per Table 4-23.

Relative strength: R0 Extremely Weak (35–150 psi, indented by thumbnail) through R6 Extremely Strong (>30,000 psi). Table 4-25. More detailed measurement by point load index or UCS tests in Chapter 9.

Drilling parameters: Automated recording of fluid pressure, feed rate, penetration rate, thrust, torque, rotation speed as function of depth. Provides supplemental characterization not yet standard practice.
key_points: RQD = (Σ pieces > 100 mm) / total core length × 100%; 0–25 very poor to 90–100 excellent
Rock types: igneous (solidified melt), sedimentary (deposited/lithified), metamorphic (transformed)
Relative strength R0 (35–150 psi, thumbnail) through R6 (>30,000 psi) — Table 4-25
Automated drilling parameters provide supplemental characterization but not yet standard practice
